claim: Female mosquitoes need a blood meal to reproduce.
source: Female mosquitoes need a blood meal to reproduce, and in obtaining this essential nutrient they transmit deadly pathogens.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about mosquito biology.

claim: Female mosquitoes transmit deadly pathogens while obtaining blood meals.
source: Female mosquitoes need a blood meal to reproduce, and in obtaining this essential nutrient they transmit deadly pathogens.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about disease transmission.

claim: Blood feeding remains poorly understood due to technological limitations.
source: Although crucial for the spread of mosquito-borne diseases, blood feeding remains poorly understood due to technological limitations.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the study in the abstract.

claim: Studies often expose human subjects to assess mosquito biting behavior.
source: Indeed, studies often expose human subjects to assess biting behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by multiple citations in the introduction.

claim: The biteOscope attracts mosquitoes to a host mimic which they bite to obtain an artificial blood meal.
source: Here, we present the biteOscope, a device that attracts mosquitoes to a host mimic which they bite to obtain an artificial blood meal.
evidence: This is the main description of the device presented in the abstract.

claim: The host mimic is transparent, allowing high-resolution imaging of the feeding mosquito.
source: The host mimic is transparent, allowing high-resolution imaging of the feeding mosquito.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated throughout the figures.

claim: Machine learning was used to extract detailed behavioral statistics describing locomotion, pose, biting, and feeding dynamics of four mosquito species.
source: Using machine learning, we extract detailed behavioral statistics describing the locomotion, pose, biting, and feeding dynamics of Aedes aegypti, Aedes albopictus, Anopheles stephensi, and Anopheles coluzzii.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and detailed in the methods and results sections.

claim: DEET repels Anopheles coluzzii upon contact with their legs.
source: In addition to characterizing behavioral patterns, we discover that the common insect repellent DEET repels Anopheles coluzzii upon contact with their legs.
evidence: This is stated as a discovery in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: Flying toward a host is relatively well characterized in mosquitoes.
source: The initial step in obtaining a blood meal, flying toward a host, is relatively well characterized (Dekker and Cardé, 2011; McMeniman et al., 2014; van Breugel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Steps that unfold after a mosquito has landed on a host are much less understood than host-seeking flight.
source: The steps that unfold after a mosquito has landed on a host, however, are much less understood.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a knowledge gap.

claim: Once landed, mosquitoes exhibit exploratory bouts during which the legs and proboscis frequently contact the skin.
source: Once landed, mosquitoes exhibit exploratory bouts during which the legs and proboscis frequently contact the skin (Jones and Pilitt, 1973; De Jong and Knols, 1995; Clements, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Receptors involved in contact-dependent sensing are present on mosquito legs and proboscis.
source: An increasing body of literature reports the presence of receptors involved in contact-dependent sensing on the legs and proboscis (Sparks et al., 2013; Matthews et al., 2019; Dennis et al., 2019), suggesting that these appendages evaluate the skin surface and thus serve an important role in bite-site selection.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Mosquito legs and proboscis serve an important role in bite-site selection.
source: An increasing body of literature reports the presence of receptors involved in contact-dependent sensing on the legs and proboscis (Sparks et al., 2013; Matthews et al., 2019; Dennis et al., 2019), suggesting that these appendages evaluate the skin surface and thus serve an important role in bite-site selection.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion based on cited literature.

claim: The role and mechanism of contact-dependent sensing in blood feeding is largely unclear.
source: Yet, the role and mechanism of contact-dependent sensing in blood feeding is largely unclear (Benton, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The skin-piercing labrum serves as a chemosensory organ guiding blood feeding.
source: In addition to the body parts that come in contact with the skin surface, the skin piercing labrum also serves as a chemosensory organ, guiding blood feeding in currently unknown ways (Lee, 1974; Werner-Reiss et al., 1999; Jove et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Nutrition, hydration, and pathogen infections have been hypothesized to affect blood feeding behavior.
source: Nutrition, hydration, and pathogen infections, for instance, have been hypothesized to affect blood feeding behavior, for example by altering feeding avidity (i.e. number of feeding attempts) or the size of the meal taken (Rossignol et al., 1984; Choumet et al., 2012; Cator et al., 2013; Vantaux et al., 2015; Hagan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The effects of physiology on blood feeding behavior remain a matter of debate due to a lack of standardized assays.
source: These topics, however, remain a matter of debate, due to a lack of (standardized) assays to measure mosquito behavior (Stanczyk et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Very few assays to characterize the blood-feeding behavior of mosquitoes exist apart from olfactometers and flight chambers.
source: Yet, apart from olfactometers and other flight chambers, very few assays to characterize the blood-feeding behavior of mosquitoes exist (Geier and Boeckh, 1999; Verhulst et al., 2011; McMeniman et al., 2014; van Breugel et al., 2015; Murray et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Studies often expose human subjects to quantify the number of landings and/or bites, or the time it takes to complete a blood meal, and score experimental outcomes by hand.
source: Due to this paucity of assays, studies often expose human subjects to quantify the number of landings and/or bites, or the time it takes to complete a blood meal, and score experimental outcomes by hand (Jones and Pilitt, 1973; Ribeiro, 2000; Moreira et al., 2009; DeGennaro et al., 2013; Dennis et al., 2019; Hughes et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The use of humans as bait constrains the number and type of experiments that can be done.
source: The use of humans as bait constrains the number and type of experiments that can be done (e.g. prohibiting the use of infected mosquitoes) and limits the type, detail, and throughput of measurements that can be made.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a limitation of current methods.

claim: The opaque nature of skin prevents the visualization of the stylets after piercing the skin.
source: Furthermore, the opaque nature of skin prevents the visualization of the stylets after piercing the skin leaving this aspect of blood feeding almost entirely unstudied, except for one notable study using intravital imaging of dissected mouse skin (Choumet et al., 2012) and two much earlier descriptions (Gordon and Lumsden, 1939; Griffiths and Gordon, 1952).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Heat is a dominant factor in short-range mosquito attraction.
source: Heat is a dominant factor in short-range mosquito attraction and can be used to attract mosquitoes to a surface and elicit probing behavior (Healy et al., 2002; Corfas and Vosshall, 2015; Zermoglio et al., 2017; Greppi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: Heat can be used to attract mosquitoes to a surface and elicit probing behavior.
source: Heat is a dominant factor in short-range mosquito attraction and can be used to attract mosquitoes to a surface and elicit probing behavior (Healy et al., 2002; Corfas and Vosshall, 2015; Zermoglio et al., 2017; Greppi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: ATP, osmotic pressure similar to blood, and sodium ions are sufficient to induce Aedes mosquitoes to feed to full engorgement.
source: To elicit blood feeding in a transparent medium, we use adenosine triphosphate (ATP) as a strong phagostimulant, which, together with an osmotic pressure similar to that of blood and the presence of sodium ions, is sufficient to induce Aedes mosquitoes to feed to full engorgement (Galun et al., 1963; Duvall et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: Anopheles require sodium ions and a tonicity similar to blood to feed to full engorgement.
source: Anopheles also require sodium ions and a tonicity similar to blood to feed to full engorgement, but interestingly their feeding rate on artificial meals is independent of ATP (Galun et al., 1985).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Anopheles feeding rate on artificial meals is independent of ATP.
source: Anopheles also require sodium ions and a tonicity similar to blood to feed to full engorgement, but interestingly their feeding rate on artificial meals is independent of ATP (Galun et al., 1985).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Ae. aegypti mosquitoes show strong attraction to the bite substrate.
source: Figure 1B demonstrates that Ae. aegypti mosquitoes show strong attraction to the bite substrate (surface indicated using a dashed line) and spend more time on its surface compared to the surrounding wall.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B as a heatmap of mosquito presence.

claim: Ae. aegypti spend more time on the bite substrate surface compared to the surrounding wall.
source: Figure 1B demonstrates that Ae. aegypti mosquitoes show strong attraction to the bite substrate (surface indicated using a dashed line) and spend more time on its surface compared to the surrounding wall.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The biteOscope enables visualization of the stylet as it evaluates the artificial meal.
source: Imaging the stylet (Videos 1 and 5) as it evaluates the artificial meal reveals the striking dexterity of the organ as it rapidly bends, extends, and retracts—aspects of feeding that normally remain hidden inside the skin.
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Videos 1 and 5.

claim: The stylet rapidly bends, extends, and retracts during feeding.
source: Imaging the stylet (Videos 1 and 5) as it evaluates the artificial meal reveals the striking dexterity of the organ as it rapidly bends, extends, and retracts—aspects of feeding that normally remain hidden inside the skin.
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Videos 1 and 5.

claim: Full engorgement is detected with a sensitivity of 81% and a specificity of 100%.
source: To determine a mosquito's engorgement status, we take advantage of the dilation of the mosquito abdomen when it takes a blood meal (Figure 1E). We determine a mosquito's body shape (excluding appendages) using an active contour model to quantify feeding dynamics and engorgement status at each timepoint of a trajectory, and detect full engorgement with a sensitivity of 81% and a specificity of 100% (see Figure 1 G1-3, Video 8, and Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on validation data.

claim: All four mosquito species land readily on the bite substrate and undertake exploratory bouts leading to full engorgement.
source: All species land readily on the bite substrate and undertake exploratory bouts leading to full engorgement in 18%, 7%, 4%, and 14% of all trajectories and 46%, 22%, 10%, and 31% of all >10 second trajectories, for Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus, An. stephensi, and An. coluzzii, respectively, when offered a meal consisting of 1 mM ATP in phosphate buffered saline (PBS).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental data.

claim: Ae. aegypti engorge to full repletion in 18% of all trajectories when offered 1 mM ATP in PBS.
source: All species land readily on the bite substrate and undertake exploratory bouts leading to full engorgement in 18%, 7%, 4%, and 14% of all trajectories and 46%, 22%, 10%, and 31% of all >10 second trajectories, for Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus, An. stephensi, and An. coluzzii, respectively, when offered a meal consisting of 1 mM ATP in phosphate buffered saline (PBS).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental data.

claim: Ae. albopictus engorge to full repletion in 7% of all trajectories when offered 1 mM ATP in PBS.
source: All species land readily on the bite substrate and undertake exploratory bouts leading to full engorgement in 18%, 7%, 4%, and 14% of all trajectories and 46%, 22%, 10%, and 31% of all >10 second trajectories, for Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus, An. stephensi, and An. coluzzii, respectively, when offered a meal consisting of 1 mM ATP in phosphate buffered saline (PBS).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental data.

claim: An. stephensi engorge to full repletion in 4% of all trajectories when offered 1 mM ATP in PBS.
source: All species land readily on the bite substrate and undertake exploratory bouts leading to full engorgement in 18%, 7%, 4%, and 14% of all trajectories and 46%, 22%, 10%, and 31% of all >10 second trajectories, for Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus, An. stephensi, and An. coluzzii, respectively, when offered a meal consisting of 1 mM ATP in phosphate buffered saline (PBS).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental data.

claim: An. coluzzii engorge to full repletion in 14% of all trajectories when offered 1 mM ATP in PBS.
source: All species land readily on the bite substrate and undertake exploratory bouts leading to full engorgement in 18%, 7%, 4%, and 14% of all trajectories and 46%, 22%, 10%, and 31% of all >10 second trajectories, for Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus, An. stephensi, and An. coluzzii, respectively, when offered a meal consisting of 1 mM ATP in phosphate buffered saline (PBS).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental data.

claim: Exploratory trajectories that do not lead to engorgement rarely exceed the duration of successful feeding trajectories.
source: As expected, rather short trajectories do not lead to engorgement, yet less intuitive is the observation that exploratory trajectories that do not lead to engorgement rarely exceed the duration of successful feeding trajectories (8% of non-feeding trajectories takes longer than the mean time to engorge).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of trajectory data.

claim: 8% of non-feeding trajectories take longer than the mean time to engorge.
source: As expected, rather short trajectories do not lead to engorgement, yet less intuitive is the observation that exploratory trajectories that do not lead to engorgement rarely exceed the duration of successful feeding trajectories (8% of non-feeding trajectories takes longer than the mean time to engorge).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of trajectory data.

claim: A mosquito's search for blood has a characteristic timescale that is independent of success.
source: This suggests that a mosquito's search for blood has a characteristic timescale that is independent of success, and when blood is not found within the time a typical meal takes, the search is aborted.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the trajectory duration data.

claim: PBS alone does not lead to engorgement in Ae. albopictus.
source: As PBS alone does not lead to engorgement, mosquitoes offered the PBS only feeder never engorged whereas mosquitoes interacting with the PBS + ATP feeder engorged to full repletion in the majority of cases (55%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental data.

claim: Ae. albopictus engorge to full repletion in 55% of cases when offered PBS + ATP.
source: As PBS alone does not lead to engorgement, mosquitoes offered the PBS only feeder never engorged whereas mosquitoes interacting with the PBS + ATP feeder engorged to full repletion in the majority of cases (55%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental data.

claim: Velocity of a mosquito's centroid can be used to classify locomotion behaviors with 89% accuracy.
source: The velocity of a mosquito's centroid can be used to classify locomotion behaviors (stationary, walking, flight) with high accuracy (89% see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on validation data.

claim: Trajectories on feeders without ATP have an approximately equal maximum duration as trajectories leading to full engorgement on the feeder with ATP.
source: Figure 3 presents ethograms of Ae. albopictus on these two bite substrates, and in agreement with the data in Figure 2E, shows that trajectories on feeders without ATP (non-feeding) have an approximately equal maximum duration as trajectories leading to full engorgement on the feeder with ATP.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The number of exploratory bouts mosquitoes undertook on the PBS only substrate was significantly higher compared to the PBS + ATP case.
source: While mosquitoes do not increase the duration of exploratory trajectories when not feeding to repletion, the number of exploratory bouts mosquitoes undertook on the PBS only substrate was significantly higher compared to the PBS + ATP case (Wilcoxon rank-sum test p < 0.05), resulting in a slightly longer total exploration time (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mosquitoes not finding their desired resource increase the frequency with which they initiate searches rather than the duration of individual searches.
source: This suggests that mosquitoes not finding their desired resource increase the frequency with which they initiate searches rather than the duration of individual searches.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental data on exploratory bouts.

claim: DeepLabCut was used to train a convolutional neural network to detect mosquito body parts.
source: We used a recently developed deep learning framework, DeepLabCut (Mathis et al., 2018), to train a convolutional neural network (CNN) to detect the head, proboscis, abdomen, abdominal tip, and six legs of Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: The same CNN can be used to track the body parts of both Aedes species with a mean accuracy of 11 pixels (275 micrometer).
source: Due to their morphological similarity, the same CNN can be used to track the body parts of both Aedes species with a mean accuracy of 11 pixels (275 micrometer, see Materials and methods for details) in a 4.3 × 4.3 cm field of view.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on validation data.

claim: Anterior grooming is characterized by circular motion of the forelegs followed by the proboscis, while the middle legs remain stationary.
source: Anterior grooming is characterized by circular motion of the forelegs followed by the proboscis, while the middle legs remain stationary (see Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4 and associated video.

claim: During walking, the tips of all six legs oscillate along the body axis while the proboscis explores laterally.
source: During walking, the tips of all six legs oscillate along the body axis while the proboscis explores laterally (see Figure 4—video 2), while during probing, the fore and middle legs pull toward the body and the proboscis remains stationary (see Figure 4—video 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4 and associated video.

claim: During probing, the fore and middle legs pull toward the body and the proboscis remains stationary.
source: During walking, the tips of all six legs oscillate along the body axis while the proboscis explores laterally (see Figure 4—video 2), while during probing, the fore and middle legs pull toward the body and the proboscis remains stationary (see Figure 4—video 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4 and associated video.

claim: Afify et al., 2019 observed that volatile DEET does not activate olfactory neurons in An. coluzzii.
source: Afify et al., 2019 recently observed that volatile DEET does not activate olfactory neurons in An. coluzzii and reported that An. coluzzii does not avoid DEET by smelling it (Afify et al., 2019; Afify and Potter, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: An. coluzzii does not avoid DEET by smelling it.
source: Afify et al., 2019 recently observed that volatile DEET does not activate olfactory neurons in An. coluzzii and reported that An. coluzzii does not avoid DEET by smelling it (Afify et al., 2019; Afify and Potter, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: Afify et al., 2019 proposed that DEET may prevent An. coluzzii from locating humans by masking odorants emanating from potential hosts.
source: Afify et al., 2019 proposed that DEET may prevent An. coluzzii from locating humans by masking odorants emanating from potential hosts.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: An. coluzzii land on both the DEET-coated and uncoated surface.
source: Figure 5 shows that An. coluzzii do land on both the DEET-coated and uncoated surface, and there is a moderate decrease in landing rate on the DEET-coated portion (the landing rate is 1.9 times lower, normalized for surface area).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The landing rate of An. coluzzii on DEET-coated surface is 1.9 times lower than on uncoated surface.
source: Figure 5 shows that An. coluzzii do land on both the DEET-coated and uncoated surface, and there is a moderate decrease in landing rate on the DEET-coated portion (the landing rate is 1.9 times lower, normalized for surface area).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The longest residence time observed on the DEET-coated surface was less than 6 s.
source: Furthermore, the longest residence time observed on the DEET-coated surface was less than 6 s, whereas individual An. coluzzii spent up to 52 s on the uncoated surface.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental data.

claim: Individual An. coluzzii spent up to 52 s on the uncoated surface.
source: Furthermore, the longest residence time observed on the DEET-coated surface was less than 6 s, whereas individual An. coluzzii spent up to 52 s on the uncoated surface.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental data.

claim: An. coluzzii approach and land on the DEET-coated surface, but avoid prolonged contact with it.
source: From these data, we conclude that An. coluzzii do approach and land on the DEET-coated surface, but avoid (prolonged) contact with it, indicating that An. coluzzii indeed is not strongly repelled by volatile DEET at very close range, yet avoids it on contact.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: An. coluzzii is not strongly repelled by volatile DEET at very close range.
source: From these data, we conclude that An. coluzzii do approach and land on the DEET-coated surface, but avoid (prolonged) contact with it, indicating that An. coluzzii indeed is not strongly repelled by volatile DEET at very close range, yet avoids it on contact.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: 25 out of 34 trajectories in which An. coluzzii visited the DEET area consisted of 'touch and go' events.
source: The 34 trajectories in which An. coluzzii visited the DEET area consisted of 25 'touch and go' events in which an individual approached the DEET surface in flight, landed, and immediately took off after first contact (residence time on DEET surface <0.5 second, see Video 11 for a typical 'touch and go' event played at 1/4 speed).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental data.

claim: In 9 trajectories, An. coluzzii landed outside the DEET area and moved onto it.
source: In the remaining nine trajectories, An. coluzzii landed outside the DEET area and moved onto it (see Figure 5 and Video 12), the reverse scenario in which a mosquito would land on the DEET surface and move onto the non-coated surface was never observed.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental data.

claim: The reverse scenario in which a mosquito would land on the DEET surface and move onto the non-coated surface was never observed.
source: In the remaining nine trajectories, An. coluzzii landed outside the DEET area and moved onto it (see Figure 5 and Video 12), the reverse scenario in which a mosquito would land on the DEET surface and move onto the non-coated surface was never observed.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental data.

claim: The legs of An. coluzzii came in contact with the DEET surface in all cases where mosquitoes moved from non-coated to DEET-coated surface.
source: We observed that the legs of individuals came in contact with the DEET surface in all cases, whereas the proboscis only came in contact with the DEET surface in 5/9 cases (in cases where no proboscis contact was observed, the entire proboscis remained outside the boarders of the DEET-treated area).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on body part tracking data.

claim: The proboscis only came in contact with the DEET surface in 5/9 cases where mosquitoes moved from non-coated to DEET-coated surface.
source: We observed that the legs of individuals came in contact with the DEET surface in all cases, whereas the proboscis only came in contact with the DEET surface in 5/9 cases (in cases where no proboscis contact was observed, the entire proboscis remained outside the boarders of the DEET-treated area).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on body part tracking data.

claim: An. coluzzii are repelled upon contact with DEET, and this behavior is mediated by sensilla on the legs, and likely not the proboscis.
source: Together, these observations demonstrate that An. coluzzii are indeed repelled upon contact with DEET, and indicate that this behavior is mediated by sensilla on the legs, and likely not the proboscis.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the body part tracking data.

claim: The biteOscope provides an alternative for current methods using human subjects or mice to study mosquito blood feeding.
source: The biteOscope provides an alternative for current methods using human subjects or mice to study mosquito blood feeding.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The elimination of the need for a human subject opens new avenues of research, including allowing blood-feeding studies with pathogen-infected mosquitoes.
source: The elimination of the need for a human subject opens new avenues of research, for example allowing blood-feeding studies with pathogen-infected mosquitoes, enabling precise surface manipulations and characterization of the associated behavior, and facilitates the use of high-resolution imaging and machine-learning-based image analysis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a benefit of the biteOscope.

claim: Mathematical models suggest that pathogen-induced changes in bite behavior can have important implications for pathogen transmission.
source: Gaining such insights is of high epidemiological relevance, as mathematical models suggest that (pathogen induced) changes in bite behavior can have important implications for pathogen transmission (Cator et al., 2014; Abboubakar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Contact-based repellency by DEET may be conserved across Anopheles and Aedes mosquitoes.
source: Together, these observations suggest that contact-based repellency may be conserved across Anopheles and Aedes mosquitoes and thus may be a potentially interesting target for the design of new repellents.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Volatile DEET activates olfactory neurons in Ae. aegypti.
source: However, in contrast to An. coluzzii, olfactory neurons of Ae. aegypti are activated by volatile DEET (Davis and Rebert, 1972; Boeckh et al., 1996; Stanczyk et al., 2010) and Ae. aegypti has been reported to avoid volatile DEET in recent studies (Stanczyk et al., 2013; Afify and Potter, 2020) (in contrast, an earlier study reported attraction of Ae. aegypti by DEET [Dogan et al., 1999]).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Ae. aegypti has been reported to avoid volatile DEET in recent studies.
source: However, in contrast to An. coluzzii, olfactory neurons of Ae. aegypti are activated by volatile DEET (Davis and Rebert, 1972; Boeckh et al., 1996; Stanczyk et al., 2010) and Ae. aegypti has been reported to avoid volatile DEET in recent studies (Stanczyk et al., 2013; Afify and Potter, 2020) (in contrast, an earlier study reported attraction of Ae. aegypti by DEET [Dogan et al., 1999]).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Ae. aegypti is repelled by DEET upon leg contact.
source: Our findings regarding An. coluzzii are in agreement with observations in Ae. aegypti which are also repelled by DEET upon leg contact (DeGennaro et al., 2013; Dennis et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The biteOscope has a relatively modest price tag of 900–3500 USD depending on the configuration.
source: It has a relatively modest price tag (900–3500 USD depending on the configuration), uses readily available materials and components, and when disassembled fits in a backpack—characteristics we hope will facilitate adoption.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: When disassembled, the biteOscope fits in a backpack.
source: It has a relatively modest price tag (900–3500 USD depending on the configuration), uses readily available materials and components, and when disassembled fits in a backpack—characteristics we hope will facilitate adoption.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Mosquitoes aged 6–25 days old were used for behavioral experiments.
source: Mosquitoes aged 6–25 days old were used for behavioral experiments.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Experiments using Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus were performed during light hours.
source: Experiments using Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus were performed during light hours, while experiments with An. stephensi and An. coluzzii were performed during dark hours.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Experiments with An. stephensi and An. coluzzii were performed during dark hours.
source: Experiments using Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus were performed during light hours, while experiments with An. stephensi and An. coluzzii were performed during dark hours.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Approximately 350 images were used to train the Aedes dataset for body part tracking.
source: Approximately 350 images were used to train the Aedes dataset, while approximately 300 images were used for the Anopheles dataset.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Approximately 300 images were used to train the Anopheles dataset for body part tracking.
source: Approximately 350 images were used to train the Aedes dataset, while approximately 300 images were used for the Anopheles dataset.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The mean accuracy of body part tracking for Aedes was 11 pixels (275 µm) in a 4.3 × 4.3 cm field of view.
source: Averaged across shuffles training yielded an accuracy, defined as the mean average Euclidean error between the manual labels and predicted labels, of 11 pixels (275 µm) and six pixels (150 µm) in a 4.3 × 4.3 cm field of view, for Aedes and Anopheles, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section based on validation data.

claim: The mean accuracy of body part tracking for Anopheles was six pixels (150 µm) in a 4.3 × 4.3 cm field of view.
source: Averaged across shuffles training yielded an accuracy, defined as the mean average Euclidean error between the manual labels and predicted labels, of 11 pixels (275 µm) and six pixels (150 µm) in a 4.3 × 4.3 cm field of view, for Aedes and Anopheles, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section based on validation data.

claim: Both Anopheles species quickly concentrate the obtained meal by excreting liquid.
source: Both Anopheles species quickly concentrate the obtained meal by excreting liquid (visible as a growing excretion droplet), Aedes excrete small droplets as well, yet to a much smaller extent.
evidence: This is stated in the caption for Video 4.

claim: Aedes excrete small droplets during feeding, yet to a much smaller extent than Anopheles.
source: Both Anopheles species quickly concentrate the obtained meal by excreting liquid (visible as a growing excretion droplet), Aedes excrete small droplets as well, yet to a much smaller extent.
evidence: This is stated in the caption for Video 4.

claim: There is a clear heterogeneity in the number of times a mosquito visits the surface among individuals from the same population raised under identical conditions.
source: Figure 3 furthermore shows a strong behavioral heterogeneity between individual mosquitoes. While all individuals are from the same mosquito population (and raised and maintained under identical conditions) and interact with the same bite substrate, there is a clear heterogeneity in the number of times a mosquito visits the surface (Figure 3C, middle panel), the amount of time she spends exploring the surface (Figure 3C, left panel), and the behaviors they engage in.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Ae. albopictus had a lower landing rate on vertically mounted substrates compared to those mounted in the floor.
source: We noted that orientation of the bite substrate affects both the landing rate of mosquitoes (e.g. Ae. albopictus had a lower landing rate on vertically mounted substrates compared to those mounted in the floor) and their orientation (on vertical surfaces mosquitoes aligned with gravity, head up bottom down).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section based on observations.
